implementation_notes: TypeScript adds types to the existing JavaScript mechanisms rather than new machinery: the context is an interface (RequestContext) and the carrier is AsyncLocalStorage<RequestContext>, so getStore() returns the typed object and a misspelled field is a compile error; a typed accessor function keeps the undefined check in one place. In NestJS the same shape comes from the framework - a provider (or controller) declared with Scope.REQUEST, or the injected REQUEST token, is instantiated per request and handed to consumers by the DI container. The classic explicit context parameter survives only where the runtime lacks async context tracking (browsers, some serverless runtimes), and there structural typing makes it cheap and safe.
pitfalls: An accessor typed as RequestContext that reads AsyncLocalStorage must still handle undefined for code called outside a request; casting it away with 'as' moves the failure to runtime.
A request-scoped provider bubbles the scope up the injection chain (NestJS Scope.REQUEST), so one request-scoped dependency makes its whole consumer graph request-scoped and measurably slower.
